Exceptionally rigorous dataset construction with multi-stage annotation pipeline (writing → peer review → dual independent validation) ensuring unambiguous ground truth
Comprehensive evaluation spanning 13+ LLMs and vision-language models with variance analysis and prompt sensitivity studies
Identifies important failure modes and insights: BPE tokenization issues, 10%+ recognition-localization gap, assembly failures in generation, ineffectiveness of vision representations

weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily a dataset paper using standard annotation methodologies without algorithmic or methodological innovations expected for top-tier venues
Modest dataset scale (200-400 instances per task, 3,600 total recognition instances) relative to modern benchmarks; insufficient for training large models

No inter-annotator agreement metrics despite multi-annotator pipeline; missing confidence intervals and statistical significance testing

Dataset composition concerns: <40 atom restriction not justified; no difficulty distribution analysis; generalization to larger molecules unexplored; UniChem sourcing biases unexamined
Extended set quality unvalidated: simplified pipeline (1 annotator + 1 validator) creates unknown accuracy degradation vs. core set; results primarily on core set only
Limited comparative context: minimal discussion of existing molecule-language datasets; no user study validating task relevance for chemists; no guidance for practitioners on model improvements
Dramatic performance variance across editing task categories (30-100% accuracy by category, Table S2) remains unexplained and suggests potential design issues or exceptionally hard subcategories

strengths: Rigorous multi-stage annotation pipeline for editing/generation tasks with expert chemistry validation, ensuring high-quality, unambiguous labels
Comprehensive baseline evaluation across diverse LLMs and vision-language models with detailed results and variance analysis
Clear identification of concrete technical limitations (BPE tokenization causing atom enumeration errors) in LLMs for molecular tasks
Well-designed multi-modal benchmark supporting SMILES, images, and ideally graphs as input representations
High transparency with clear documentation, annotation standards, reproducible examples, and promised code/data release
weaknesses: Weak practical relevance: molecular structure recognition is solved by RDKit; no evidence that LLM-based editing/generation addresses real chemical workflows or bottlenecks
Limited dataset scale (200 examples per task, 18 recognition tasks with sparsity) and narrow chemical space (molecules <40 atoms, ~24 non-H atoms average, far from realistic drug-like complexity)
No methodological novelty—pure benchmark paper with no new models, algorithms, or annotation techniques; limited novelty for top-tier venue standards

Incomplete experimental design missing critical baselines: chemistry-specific models relegated to appendix with minimal analysis, no fine-tuned models, no specialized molecular generators, no alternative output formats (IUPAC, InChI)

Shallow results analysis: heterogeneous editing performance (30% chirality vs. 100% charge) unexplored; generation vs. editing gap (43% vs. 85.5%) not analyzed; tokenization issue identified but unsolved; no inter-annotator agreement metrics reported
Overstated claims about identifying AI system shortcomings without establishing practical importance; assumes LLMs are appropriate tools for tasks better solved by specialized cheminformatics tools
Questionable evaluation metrics: exact SMILES matching too strict and lacks chemical similarity granularity; vision-language evaluation relies on manual validation and imperfect OCR

Missing ablations and analyses: no scaling studies, no few-shot/chain-of-thought prompting experiments, limited investigation into why vision models underperform, no transfer learning analysis across datasets

strengths: Addresses important gap in molecule-language AI with first comprehensive benchmark for recognition, editing, and generation tasks
Exemplary data curation: rigorous multi-stage annotation for editing/generation with automated ground truth for recognition; emphasis on deterministic unambiguous answers critical for chemistry
Comprehensive evaluation: 11+ LLMs, vision-language models, multiple modalities (SMILES, images), chemistry-specific models, with detailed variance and sensitivity analysis

Thorough error analysis: identifies specific failure modes including BPE tokenization issues for atom enumeration and assembly failures in generation; reveals that GPT-5 only achieves 43% on generation despite 86.2% on recognition
Well-designed tasks reflecting real chemist workflows with 18 diverse recognition subtasks spanning topology, functional groups, and stereochemistry
Excellent presentation: clear writing, informative figures, comprehensive 27-page appendix with detailed annotations, guidelines, and full results enabling reproducibility
Honest results documenting stark limitations of current models and providing actionable insights for future work
weaknesses: Dataset size is modest: only 200 core instances per task (extended sets also 200 with simplified annotation); unclear how well this scales for training-based approaches or to larger molecules; no learning curves or sample efficiency analysis

Critical results inadequately explained: chemistry-specific LLMs fail almost entirely but discussion relegated to appendix with minimal investigation; large recognition-to-localization gap (>10% for most models) not systematically analyzed; why domain-specific models underperform general models deserves main text treatment

Graph-language modality missing: authors acknowledge no practical models exist, but this leaves important molecular representation unexplored and contradicts claims of supporting 'different molecular representations'

Insufficient analysis of task difficulty: no systematic characterization of which factors make tasks hard/easy; no difficulty ranking across tasks or analysis of performance by molecule properties; limits ability to identify bottlenecks
Evaluation metrics coarse: pass@1 accuracy provides no partial credit; no analysis of error distribution in generation (why 69% valid SMILES but only 43% correct?); no graduated scoring

Vision-language results potentially misleading: GPT Image 1 achieving 0% on generation likely reflects poor model choice rather than fundamental limitations; OCR validation introduces additional error source (2.72% false positive rate)

Annotation quality assurance gaps: no inter-annotator agreement statistics; only 2 validators per instance with no analysis of validator error rates; particularly concerning for complex generation descriptions

Missing baselines: no comparison to specialized chemistry generation models (e.g., domain-specific molecular generators); no non-learning baselines (rule-based, template systems); limits claims about current methods' limitations
Generalization concerns: all molecules from UniChem; maximum 40 non-H atoms; no analysis of transfer to larger molecules or different chemical spaces; unclear if findings generalize beyond this scope

strengths: Exceptionally rigorous dataset construction with multi-stage annotation pipeline, peer review, and independent validation ensuring high-quality deterministic outputs
Comprehensive evaluation spanning 15+ diverse models (general-purpose LLMs, reasoning-specialized, vision-language) with honest reporting of limitations
Well-motivated tasks grounded in real chemistry workflows (recognition, editing, generation) with clear practical relevance

Detailed error analysis revealing systematic failure modes (tokenization issues causing atom enumeration errors, stereochemistry recognition failures, chain length mistakes) with concrete mechanistic insights
Multiple modality support (SMILES, molecular images, graphs) and thorough supplementary analyses (prompt sensitivity, variance analysis, SELFIES evaluation, chemistry-specific LLM evaluation)
Clear identification of significant limitations even in state-of-the-art models (GPT-5: 86.2% recognition, 43% generation) providing valuable benchmarking resource
Reproducibility considerations including model snapshots, variance analysis, and promised release of dataset and code
weaknesses: Limited dataset scale with only 200 core examples per task raises questions about statistical significance and generalization; lacks analysis of dataset size sufficiency
Circular task design for recognition: using RDKit to generate ground truth then evaluating LLMs on RDKit-solvable tasks limits clarity on meaningful reasoning evaluation
Small molecule complexity scope (mostly <40 non-H atoms) insufficient for real pharmaceutical compounds; lacks evaluation on truly complex polycyclic systems
Extensive documentation of failure modes but limited mechanistic analysis or proposed solutions; no experiments with potential improvements (chain-of-thought, few-shot learning, fine-tuning)

Vision-language evaluation concerns: GPT Image 1 performs catastrophically (0% generation) with limited analysis; only one image model evaluated; overlaid atom indices may not reflect realistic scenarios
Weak practical motivation: unclear when chemists would use LLMs to recognize structures they already possess; limited connection between solving tasks and downstream chemistry applications
Limited novelty: primarily engineering/curation contribution rather than methodological innovation; task formulation is relatively straightforward application of existing concepts
Missing key baselines and comparisons: no traditional chemistry software baselines, simple heuristics, retrieval methods, or systematic analysis of why chemistry-specific LLMs fail dramatically
Evaluation strictness concerns: exact SMILES match is overly stringent given multiple valid representations exist; Tanimoto similarity deemphasized; OCR has 2.7% false positive rate
Modest downstream improvements with structure analysis (~5% on BBBP/BACE) and limited evidence that solving MolLangBench enables real scientific applications

strengths: Rigorous annotation pipeline with multiple review rounds and independent validation demonstrating genuine care for dataset quality
Comprehensive evaluation across 16+ models with robustness analysis (variance, pass@k metrics) and detailed error categorization
Clear technical documentation of identified LLM limitations (BPE tokenization, atom enumeration issues)
Systematic evaluation across multiple modalities (SMILES strings, images, molecular graphs)
Transparent methodology with extensive appendices enabling assessment of design choices
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Purely a benchmarking exercise applying existing models to existing task types without methodological innovation

Identified problems without solutions: Well-documents tokenization/atom enumeration issues but provides no mitigation strategies or forward guidance
Incomplete quality control: Extended dataset (200 instances) uses simplified annotation with single validation; mixing core and extended results in main paper

Limited scope: No consideration of reactions, synthesis, molecular properties; restricted to simple modification and generation tasks

strengths: Exceptionally rigorous dataset curation with a sophisticated 3-stage annotation pipeline (writing → peer review → independent dual validation) and clear quality control standards

Comprehensive evaluation spanning 14+ language models including reasoning-specialized variants, multiple molecular representations (SMILES, images, graphs), and detailed error analysis with specific failure modes identified
Well-motivated and timely contribution addressing the important molecule-language interface problem, grounded in realistic chemist workflows and with clear practical applications
Actionable insights into specific limitations (e.g., atom enumeration failures due to BPE tokenization, persistent stereochemistry weaknesses) that could guide future architecture design

Excellent presentation and transparency, including variance analysis (A.14), detailed error categorization (Table 3, A.19), ablation studies (SELFIES, prompt sensitivity), and connection to downstream tasks (A.13)

Careful recognition task design with balanced distributions and deliberately challenging cases (non-adjacent bonds in SMILES, distant atoms) that probe genuine structural understanding rather than surface patterns
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty - primarily a dataset/benchmark contribution that applies existing LLMs to a structured task domain without proposing novel methods, architectures, or training strategies

Dataset scale and scope constraints: 200 instances per task is modest by modern standards; molecules restricted to <40 heavy atoms; generation descriptions artificially lengthy (mean 131 words) optimized for human rather than LLM comprehension

Insufficient analysis of solutions - paper identifies that models fail but provides minimal guidance on how to fix problems; no experiments with fine-tuning, architecture modifications, or specialized tokenization schemes

Evaluation design concerns: (1) Image-based recognition unfairly simplified by directly highlighting atom indices, eliminating enumeration challenge; (2) Harsh generation metrics allowing no credit for structurally similar molecules (high Tanimoto similarity); (3) Chemistry-specific LLM evaluation potentially compromised by insufficient prompt engineering setup

Critical missing elements: no human performance baseline for calibration; dataset and code not yet released despite claims (links are blank); limited analysis of which task categories/structures are hardest; no proposed directions for solutions

Incomplete comparisons to specialized baselines - missing evaluation of domain-specific molecular models (e.g., MolT5, Text2Mol) and fine-tuned systems; variance analysis restricted to single model (o3) due to cost constraints
